nameStory: The waxy-fruited hawthorn gets its name from the distinctive waxy coating that covers its small red fruits, giving them a frosted or pruned appearance. This waxy bloom on the berries is so characteristic that botanists also call it the 'frosted hawthorn.' The coating helps protect the fruit from moisture loss and gives it an almost artificial, polished look that catches the eye.
description: Waxy-fruited hawthorn is a small thorny tree or large shrub in the rose family, typically growing 10-20 feet tall. Like other hawthorns, it produces clusters of white flowers in spring followed by small red berries in fall. What sets it apart is the distinctive waxy coating on its fruits that gives them a frosted appearance. It's a relatively uncommon hawthorn species in New England, making it an exciting find for plant enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small red berries with a distinctive waxy, frosted coating that feels slightly slippery to the touch and gives fruits an almost artificial shine

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: White flowers in flat-topped clusters during late spring, each flower has 5 petals and numerous stamens with a sweet, slightly musky fragrance

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree or large shrub reaching 10-20 feet, with an irregular, often multi-stemmed form and thorny branches

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Alternate leaves that are oval with shallow lobes and serrated edges, feeling somewhat thick and leathery compared to other hawthorns

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Gray-brown bark that becomes scaly with age, and sharp thorns up to 2 inches long on branches and trunk

habitat: Waxy-fruited hawthorn grows in open woodlands, forest edges, and old fields throughout New England, preferring well-drained soils. It's often found along woodland borders where it gets partial sun, and occasionally in abandoned pastures or along country roadsides. This species is quite rare in New England, so finding one is special - it's more common in areas with limestone-rich soils.

seasonality.spring: White flower clusters bloom in May, filling the air with their sweet fragrance and attracting bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Green fruits develop after flowering, and the thorny branches provide nesting sites for birds seeking protection.
seasonality.fall: The characteristic waxy red berries ripen and become most noticeable, while leaves may turn yellow-orange before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny branches reveal the tree's structure, and any remaining waxy berries stand out against the snow, attracting winter birds.

funFact: The waxy coating on this hawthorn's berries is so distinctive that you can actually feel it - run your finger over a ripe fruit and you'll notice it feels slightly slippery, almost like it's been waxed like an apple at the grocery store, which is nature's way of waterproofing the seeds inside!
confusionNotes: With only 14 recorded observations in New England, waxy-fruited hawthorn is easily confused with the more common dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn. The key difference is in the fruits - squeeze a ripe berry gently and feel for that distinctive waxy, slippery coating that other hawthorns lack. Memory trick: 'Waxy feels slick, other hawthorns stick.'
contextualKnowledge: Hawthorns are notoriously difficult to identify, with botanists debating whether many forms are separate species or just variations of the same plant. Some experts consider waxy-fruited hawthorn to be several different species rather than just one, which explains why field guides sometimes disagree about hawthorn identification.
compareHints: Among New England's many hawthorn species, waxy-fruited hawthorn stands out primarily for its distinctively coated berries - no other local hawthorn has that waxy, frosted appearance on the fruits. While dotted hawthorn has spotted berries and cockspur hawthorn has extremely long thorns, waxy-fruited hawthorn's calling card is always that slippery, wax-coated fruit. The berries are also typically a bit more rounded than the often pear-shaped fruits of other hawthorns.

Among New England's many hawthorn species, cockspur stands out with the longest thorns - much longer than dotted hawthorn's short spines or Washington hawthorn's modest thorns.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, big-fruit hawthorn stands out for its notably larger berries and earlier bloom time.
Among New England hawthorns, large-thorn hawthorn stands out primarily for its exceptionally long, straight thorns that dwarf those of relatives like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn.

Among the many hawthorn species in New England, Washington hawthorn stands out with its distinctly triangular, deeply lobed leaves (rather than the more oval or rounded leaves of species like dotted hawthorn).

Among New England's many hawthorns, fireberry hawthorn stands out for its golden-yellow unripe fruits - most relatives like dotted hawthorn or cockspur hawthorn have green unripe fruits that turn red.
Large-flowered cockspurthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives primarily by its notably large flowers - nearly twice the size of most other hawthorns.

Among New England hawthorns, Biltmore hawthorn stands out for its green, yellow, or orange fruits - most others like dotted hawthorn, common hawthorn, and cockspur hawthorn have red fruits.

Cleft-leaved hawthorn's leaves are much more deeply divided than most New England hawthorns - while dotted hawthorn has shallow lobes and cockspur hawthorn has barely any lobes at all, this species' leaves are cut nearly to the midrib.

Among New England's hawthorns, pea hawthorn stands out for having the smallest fruits in the genus - significantly smaller than the cherry-sized fruits of dotted hawthorn or the larger berries of cockspur hawthorn.
Among New England's many hawthorns, downy hawthorn stands out for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - most others like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have smooth or only slightly hairy leaves.
Blanchard's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and longer thorns.

Stone's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having more deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics.
Fleshy hawthorn stands out from its many hawthorn relatives by having the juiciest, most succulent berries in the group.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, scarlet hawthorn is distinguished by its particularly prominent thorns and bright red fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorn species, Schuette's hawthorn is distinguished by subtle characteristics that require expert identification.
Northern hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less deeply lobed leaves and different fruit characteristics, though these distinctions can be subtle.
Dodge's hawthorn differs from the more common dotted hawthorn by having less prominently marked leaves and typically fewer, larger thorns.
Holmes' hawthorn is most closely related to scarlet hawthorn but distinguished by its more elongated leaves and egg-shaped rather than round fruits.
Among New England's many hawthorns, broad-leaved cockspurthorn stands out for its exceptionally broad, substantial leaves that are wider than most of its relatives.

Among New England hawthorns, poplar hawthorn stands out immediately for its broad, oval, relatively unlobed leaves - most other hawthorns like dotted hawthorn or common hawthorn have deeply cut, lobed leaves.
